prompt.title: Help map non-native species in Akita
prompt.body: Answer two quick questions and learn how to read the map in one minute.

1.title: Living things are disappearing from our ponds
1.body: The American Crayfish was brought to Japan by people in 1927, as food for American Bullfrogs. In ponds where their numbers grow, the water plants disappear and the water turns brown and cloudy. The small creatures that lived there slowly vanish too.
1.imageAlt: A drawing of the same pond in two states, side by side. On the left, a clear pond with swaying water plants, small fish, water insects and tadpoles. On the right, the water plants are gone, the water is brown and cloudy, and only an American Crayfish is left on the bottom.

2.title: But we still do not know where they are
2.body: The maps published by the national government only go down to the level of a whole city or town. They cannot tell you whether the pond next door has crayfish in it. There are also waters where crayfish have not arrived yet.
2.imageAlt: A drawing comparing two levels of map detail. On the left, a coarse map where large blocks are filled in with a single colour, even though one block holds several ponds. On the right, a fine map with a small dot on each individual pond.
2.quote: 確認情報がない場所にも、生息している可能性はあることに注意。 (Japanese original. Unofficial translation by Zaridasu: "Please note that they may also be living in places where no sighting records exist.")
2.quoteSource: Source: Ministry of the Environment website, "なぜそこら中に？　まだ大丈夫なところもあります！" (accessed August 5, 2026)
2.quoteLink: Read it on the Ministry of the Environment website

3.title: So we are making the map together
3.body: When many "I found one" reports come together, they make a map fine enough to show each single pond. That lets us decide which waters to look after first, and it turns this into a story about the pond near your home, not somewhere far away.
3.imageAlt: A drawing of people standing by the water with phones, with small dots travelling from them onto a map and building up a fine distribution map that shows each pond. Zari-kun, the crayfish mascot, watches from the side.

4.title: There are only three steps
4.body: Find it, take a photo and post it, and it appears on the map. That is all. Even without a photo, "I saw one" is still a valuable report. It takes less than a minute.
4.imageAlt: A drawing of three steps from left to right. On the left, someone spots an American Crayfish by the water. In the middle, they take a photo with a phone. On the right, a single red dot appears on the map.

5.title: Just recording it is enough
5.body: You do not need to take it home. Releasing it somewhere else is against the law, so please leave the animal where it is. If you already keep one at home, you can go on keeping it, and no paperwork is needed.
5.imageAlt: A drawing of a person crouching by the water and simply taking a photo of an American Crayfish with a phone. They are not reaching out, and they carry no bucket or net. The crayfish stays in the water.

6.title: Would you like to start?
6.body: You can look at the map right away without signing up. Zaridasu is free for everyone.
6.imageAlt: A drawing of Zari-kun, the crayfish mascot, raising a claw in welcome. Behind him are the water's edge and a map with a few red dots on it.

about.title: About This Service
about.serviceDesc: Zaridasu is a map service for sharing sighting and distribution information of invasive species (American Crayfish and American Bullfrog) in Akita Prefecture, Japan. You can contribute to local ecosystem conservation by reporting sightings, captures, traces, and agricultural damage.
about.lawSubtitle: Act for the Prevention of Damage to Ecosystems Caused by Specified Invasive Alien Species
about.dataUsageDesc: Posted data may be used for distribution surveys, ecosystem conservation research, and invasive species countermeasures in Akita Prefecture. No personally identifiable information is collected.
about.contactDesc: For bug reports, feedback, or questions, please use the contact form.
about.relatedLinks: Related Links (Ministry of the Environment, Japan)

steps.1: Tap "Post a Sighting" on the top screen
steps.2: Tap the map to select the location

faq.a1: Tap "Post a Sighting" on the top screen, then select the location on the map. Enter species, type, municipality, etc., attach a photo (optional), and submit.
faq.q2: What kind of creature is the American Crayfish?
faq.a2: The American Crayfish (Procambarus clarkii) is a widely distributed invasive species, red and large. They live in agricultural canals, rice paddies, and ponds. Since June 2023 they have been a "Conditionally Specified Invasive Alien Species". You can keep one as a pet at home just as before, with no paperwork required. However, releasing them into ponds, rivers, or other outdoor waters, and selling, buying, distributing, or importing them, are prohibited.
faq.q3: What kind of creature is the American Bullfrog?
faq.a3: The American Bullfrog (Lithobates catesbeianus) is a large frog native to North America, 15-20cm in length. They live in waterfronts and wetlands and prey on native frogs, fish, and insects. They have been a "Specified Invasive Alien Species" since 2006, so keeping, transporting, importing, selling, and releasing them are prohibited in principle (except with a permit for research and similar purposes).
faq.q4: What should I do with captured crayfish or bullfrogs?
faq.a4: You do not have to catch anything. Finding one and reporting it with a photo is enough. For the American Crayfish, catch and release on the spot is fine, but once you have taken one home, releasing it outdoors later is against the law, so please think carefully about whether you can care for it for life before taking it home. For the American Bullfrog, even taking it home requires a permit.
faq.q5: How is the information posted on Zaridasu used?
faq.a5: Posted data may be used for distribution surveys, ecosystem conservation research, and invasive species countermeasures in Akita Prefecture. No personally identifiable information is collected.

american.desc: A large crayfish native to North America. Red, 10-15cm long. Widely inhabit agricultural canals, rice paddies, and ponds, causing damage to aquatic plants and agricultural structures. A Conditionally Specified Invasive Alien Species since June 2023. You can keep one as a pet at home as before without any paperwork, but releasing it outdoors and selling, buying, distributing, or importing it are prohibited.

bullfrog.desc: A large frog native to North America. 15-20cm long with a distinctive low voice. Inhabit waterfronts, wetlands, and rice paddies, preying on native creatures. A Specified Invasive Alien Species since 2006. Unlike the American Crayfish, keeping and transporting them also requires a permit.

aiAccuracy.title: ⑤ AI Confidence → Hit Rate
aiAccuracy.note: Splits AI confidence into 4 bands and cross-checks human decisions against the AI's detected species. The confirmed species of approved posts is treated as ground truth — an operational proxy (true precision/recall needs a labeled validation set).
aiAccuracy.empty: No posts with an AI confidence score yet.
aiAccuracy.approvalRateDef: Approval rate = approved ÷ (approved + rejected). Pending is excluded from the denominator.
aiAccuracy.matchRateDef: Hit rate = (approved AND AI-detected species = confirmed species) ÷ approved.
aiAccuracy.caveat: Approval rate is inflated by auto-approval (which is confidence-gated). For an independent basis, refer to the human-reviewed hit rate.

hero.title: Your "I found one" helps protect Akita's nature.
hero.subtitle: Spot a crayfish or bullfrog? Just snap a photo and post it. Your report becomes part of the map and helps protect Akita's nature. Free forever.
hero.ctaSecondary: See the map without signing up

problem.title: What's happening in Akita's waterways
problem.item1Body: American crayfish and bullfrogs are creatures that were not originally found in Japan. They eat small creatures in rice paddies and waterways, and their numbers keep growing.
problem.item2Title: We still don't know where they are
problem.item2Body: The first step to protecting nature is knowing where they live. But Akita is big, and there aren't enough people to survey it.
problem.item3Body: One crayfish you saw on a walk. A croak you heard near a rice paddy. Each small report becomes a big clue for protecting Akita's nature.

features.title: What makes Zaridasu fun
features.mapTitle: Your report appears on the map right away
features.mapBody: Posted reports show up on the Akita map immediately. Watch the one you found become part of everyone's map.
features.aiTitle: Don't know the name? AI will tell you
features.aiBody: AI identifies creatures from photos and calls, and shares tips for better photos — so you keep learning as you go.
features.requestsTitle: Your reports are used in research
features.requestsBody: Respond to researchers asking to survey specific places. Your report directly supports surveys that protect Akita's nature.
features.gamificationTitle: The more you post, the more fun it gets
features.gamificationBody: Earn badges and climb the rankings as you post. Your progress is visible — great for creature hunts with kids, too.

how.title: Get started in 3 easy steps
how.step1Body: Spot a crayfish or bullfrog near rice paddies, waterways, or rivers. Hearing a call counts, too.
how.step2Body: Take a photo and pick the spot on the map. Done in a minute. No photo? You can still post.
how.step3Body: After a quick check, your report appears on everyone's map and is used to protect Akita's nature.

stats.title: Reports are coming in from all over Akita
stats.operator: Zaridasu is a free service built by a university student who loves Akita's nature. Collected reports support research and local government efforts to protect it.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.a1: No. Everything, including sign-up, is completely free.
faq.q2: What do I need to sign up?
faq.a2: Just an email address or a Google account. No name or address required.
faq.q3: I don't know much about wildlife. Is that OK?
faq.a3: Absolutely. AI identifies creatures from your photos and calls, and teaches you how to tell them apart — you'll learn as you go.
faq.q4: Can I post without a photo?
faq.a4: Yes. Photos are optional. "I saw one" or "I heard one" is still a valuable report.
faq.q5: Can I use it outside Akita?
faq.a5: Anyone can view the map. Reports can only be posted for sightings within Akita Prefecture.
faq.q6: Do I have to catch them?
faq.a6: No — just reporting a sighting is enough. If you do catch one, note that releasing it alive elsewhere is prohibited by law.
faq.q7: Could other people tell my home location from where I post?
faq.a7: Don't worry. The map only shows where a sighting was found, not the name or contact details of who posted it. Other people can't tell who reported it, so you can take part with peace of mind.

edu.title: Please learn about these creatures
edu.body: These creatures are covered by the Invasive Alien Species Act. For the American Bullfrog, keeping, transporting, or releasing live individuals is prohibited in principle. The American Crayfish is a "Conditionally Specified Invasive Alien Species": you may keep one at home without any paperwork, but releasing it outdoors is prohibited. This tank is only a virtual record. When you find a real one, please leave it where it is - recording it is all you need to do.

Photos that help

guide.water:
Look at a familiar waterway on your walk. Notice the water flow, plants and surroundings as well as the animals.
Recording where and when you looked helps us study the habitat.
guide.photos:
From a safe place, photograph the whole animal and its surroundings. You do not need to get too close or move an animal for a photo.
Avoid capturing faces or private addresses. A photo is optional.
guide.species:
Some species have few public records so far. If you find one near the water, record it with a photo and place. Your first record helps us understand where the species lives.
You do not need to catch or move an animal. Observe from a safe place.
guide.area: Try observing watersides in different municipalities when convenient. There is no need to make a special trip. Approved observations update the municipalities in your collection.
guide.absence:
If you looked but found nothing, record an absence observation. Include where, when and how long you searched.
Not finding an animal once does not prove it is absent from that place.

login.question: Do I need an account just to look around?
login.answer: You can view the home, map and public records without an account. Sign in to post observations and keep your own collection and badges.

status.question: Will my observation appear immediately?
status.answer: Records are published after review. Check pending or returned records from your records on My page.

safety.question: How can I observe safely?
safety.answer: Observe from safe places where entry is permitted. Watch your footing, water levels and the weather. You do not need to capture or move animals. Put safety before recording.
